title: Vector File Formats: A Practical Overview
seoTitle: Vector File Formats Explained — SVG, DXF, EPS, PDF, DST, PES
seoDescription: A practical guide to the vector formats that matter most: SVG, DXF, EPS, PDF, DST, and PES. Learn what each format is for, how it stores geometry, and when to convert.
content:
Every vector format began as a solution to one specific problem: how to describe a shape without pixels, in a way a particular machine or piece of software can understand. Once you know what problem a format was built for, choosing between them stops being guesswork. This overview covers the six formats that come up most often in design and maker work — SVG, DXF, EPS, PDF, DST and PES — and explains what each one actually stores, which tools read it, and where conversion tends to lose fidelity.

The two things a vector file stores

Before comparing formats it helps to separate two kinds of information inside any vector file. The first is geometry: paths, bezier curves, lines, arcs, and the coordinates that define them. The second is appearance: fills, strokes, stroke widths, colors, gradients, layer structure, and text. Geometry is what the shape is; appearance is what it looks like.

Formats differ enormously in how much appearance they store. EFS and PDF files happily carry embedded fonts, transparency, and gradients. DXF carries almost none of it — only geometry and layer names. Embroidery formats carry neither appearance nor free-form curves; they store ordered stitches. When you convert between formats, you are almost always moving down this ladder, and the loss that worries people is usually a loss of appearance rather than a loss of shape.

SVG — the web-native format

SVG is XML. A single file describes shapes as elements, styles as attributes or CSS, and can embed effects, animations, and fonts. That textual nature is why SVG is both powerful and bloated: an export from a design tool routinely contains editor metadata, unused groups, and coordinates carried to six decimal places.

SVG is the right choice for anything that will be viewed in a browser, embedded in an app, or fed into a cutting workflow — Cricut Design Space, Silhouette Studio, and most laser cutters accept SVG. It is the most portable vector format for 2D artwork, and the one most conversion tools use as a hub. When people say they need a "vector file" for a website, they almost always mean SVG.

DXF — geometry for machines

DXF (Drawing Exchange Format) comes from the CAD world. It stores lines, polylines, arcs, splines, and layer names as plain text, with a version-specific structure that CAD and CAM software reads directly. There are no strokes you can restyle, no embedded images, and no typographic text that will render anywhere outside a CAD environment.

DXF is the standard submission format for laser cutters, CNC routers, plasma tables, and waterjets. It is also the format where units matter most: a DXF file can declare millimetres, inches, or no unit at all, and a machine that guesses wrong will cut a part at the wrong size. Before sending DXF to a cutter, confirm that your drawing units match the machine's setup.

EPS — encapsulation with print heritage

EPS (Encapsulated PostScript) is a page description language wrapped around a single graphic. It stores true bezier curves, CMYK and spot colors, embedded fonts, and a raster preview for older software that cannot render PostScript. Print shops and Adobe applications still treat it as lingua franca, and many vinyl cutters and older RIP software read it happily.

EPS is a good choice when you need a print-ready vector with complex curves and color specification. Modern workflows often prefer PDF, but EPS remains the safest interchange format for older print equipment. When converting an EPS to SVG, watch for text that has not been outlined — without the embedded font, that text may convert as shapes or not at all.

PDF — a page, not a shape

PDF is a container. A page can hold vector paths, true text, linked images, annotations, and form fields. That flexibility makes it excellent for sharing documents and print-ready artwork, and less excellent as an isolated graphic file: if you convert a PDF to SVG, you must decide which page, which objects, and which of the appearance you intend to keep.

PDF is the default in commercial printing, and most print shops will ask for PDF/X variants for anything that runs through a press. If the goal is a standalone editable graphic, PDF is usually a detour — convert it back to SVG or AI first, then work on the shape.

DST, PES and JEF — embroidery formats

Embroidery machines do not follow paths. They receive an ordered sequence of stitches — needle penetrations with coordinates, start and stop commands, thread changes, and trims. DST is the oldest and most universal format; PES is Brother's native format and stores some object-level metadata; JEF is Janome's. All three are fundamentally machine instructions, not artwork.

This distinction explains why converting an SVG to DST requires more than a file extension change. A converter must apply stitching logic — underlay, pull compensation, density, and fill patterns — because a bare outline of a logo is not something a needle can execute. Expect to size and tune the result in embroidery software before running production.

Choosing a format in one pass

GoalBest formatWhy
Website, app, or cutting workflowSVGPortable, editable, accepted by most cutters
Laser, CNC, or CADDXFPure geometry with layers; declared units
Print productionPDF or EPSCMYK, spot colors, outlined type
Embroidery machineDST / PES / JEFOrdered stitches, thread changes
Interchange between design toolsSVG or PDFBroad support, preserves appearance

Where conversion loses fidelity

Most quality problems happen at the boundary where a format drops a feature. Moving from SVG to DXF removes strokes, gradients, and text objects; the geometry survives, but a stroked line becomes a path you must then outline. Moving from a raster image to a vector format is a different class of conversion entirely: it requires tracing, whether by hand or by a tool, and the quality of the trace is bounded by the source resolution and contrast, not by the target format.

The practical rule is to convert as late as possible and check the smallest detail in the output. Open the converted file at 400% and look at the curves, the corners, and any narrow gaps. If a shape was intended to be cut, make sure the resulting paths are closed and that no two outlines overlap in a way a cutter cannot resolve.

title: The Complete SVG Optimization Guide
seoTitle: SVG Optimization Guide — Shrink File Size Without Losing Quality
seoDescription: Learn how to reduce SVG file size by rounding coordinates, stripping editor metadata, flattening groups, and cleaning path data — without changing how the artwork looks.
content:
An SVG that looks fine on screen can still be ten times larger than it needs to be. The excess usually comes from four places: coordinates carried to absurd precision, editor metadata that no renderer uses, redundant groups and transforms, and path data that repeats points along a straight line. This guide walks through each source of bloat and the specific techniques that remove it without touching what the artwork looks like.

Why SVG files get large

Vector size is not about how complex the picture looks. It is about how many numbers the file contains and how many digits each number uses. A single path with 20,000 nodes and six-decimal coordinates can dwarf an entire illustration composed of elegant 30-node curves. Design tools frequently emit that kind of file because they round-trip every editor state — named layers, unused swatches, viewport settings, and plugin data.

The best way to understand the problem is to open the SVG in a text editor and look at a path. If you see something like d="M 12.384756 -4.293847 L 12.384756 -4.100000 L 12.384756 -3.900000", you are looking at two distinct costs: numeric precision and unnecessary intermediate points. Removing a few decimal places loses nothing a printer or screen can detect. Removing collinear points loses even less.

Step one: reduce coordinate precision

A machine can distinguish roughly 0.05 of a millimetre. Print at 300 dpi resolves about 0.08 of a millimetre. Yet many exports carry six decimals of a millimetre, which is a sub-nanometre claim. Rounding path coordinates to two or three decimals is usually invisible in output and cuts file size dramatically, because every trailing digit costs one byte in a text format and many paths repeat coordinates hundreds of times.

If your file uses viewBox units where 1 unit equals 1 pixel, two decimals is plenty; if 1 unit equals a millimetre, three decimals is generous. If you are worried about rounding drift across many small segments, apply the rounding to every coordinate once rather than repeatedly optimizing an already-rounded file.

Step two: strip editor metadata

  • Comments and descriptions — Inkscape and Illustrator both write history and tool notes that renderers ignore.
  • Editor-specific namespaces — sodipodi, inkscape, sketch, and adobe attributes are not needed by browsers or cutters.
  • Unused defs — gradients, clip paths, and symbols that nothing references.
  • Empty groups and stray elements — zero-size rectangles, anchors, and hidden groups left from editing.

These are safe removals because they do not change the rendering model. The one caution is accessibility: preserved and <desc> elements and role attributes are worth keeping. Strip the editor chatter, not the meaning.</p> <h2>Step three: flatten redundant structure</h2> <p>Design tools build hierarchy to make editing pleasant: a group that contains one group that contains one path, with a transform on each level. Rendered output collapses that structure anyway, so a file can be flattened without visual change. Nested identity transforms, empty groups, and duplicated clip paths are the usual offenders.</p> <p>Transforms are subtler. A <g transform="translate(10,10)"> around a path is harmless, but a chain of five transforms forces the renderer to compose matrices before drawing. Where it is safe, bake transforms into path coordinates and remove the wrapper. Where it is not, because the same path is reused with different transforms, consolidate the definitions instead of duplicating geometry.</p> <h2>Step four: clean the path data</h2> <p>Path data has its own predictable waste. Curves exported from tracing tools often contain points that sit on a straight line, which can be replaced by a single line command. Curved segments whose control points are collinear may have been straight lines all along. Repeated relative commands can use the implicit repetition rules of the SVG path grammar.</p> <p>Do not add points by hand to "fix" a curve after rounding; that reverses the savings. Instead, look for genuinely redundant nodes: a smooth curve that was flattened during export can often be refit with fewer, more accurate beziers. This is the one operation that benefits from visual comparison, so preview at high zoom against the original.</p> <h2>Step five: embed or remove what you do not need</h2> <p>Embedded raster images are the largest thing in many SVGs. A base64 PNG inside an SVG is not vector art; it is a picture inside a wrapper, and it inflates the file by roughly a third over the binary size. If the image is decorative, consider whether the SVG needs it at all. If the SVG is destined for a cutter, embedded images usually cannot be cut and should be removed or traced into paths.</p> <p>Fonts are the other embedding trap. Converting text to outlines guarantees the file renders anywhere and eliminates font dependencies, at the cost of a longer path list. If the SVG is for web display and the font is loaded by the page, keeping live text may be smaller. If the SVG is for production, outline it and remove the font block.</p> <h2>A safe optimization order</h2> <ol><li>Back up the original before editing.</li><li>Remove comments, editor namespaces, and metadata.</li><li>Delete unreferenced defs, symbols, and empty groups.</li><li>Flatten unnecessary group and transform nesting.</li><li>Round coordinates once, to a precision that fits the intended output.</li><li>Collapse redundant path commands and collinear points.</li><li>Outline or subset text according to the destination.</li><li>Compare the optimized file against the original at 400% zoom before shipping.</li></ol> <p>Run the sequence in that order and most files shed a large fraction of their bytes in the first three steps alone. If a later step makes the file bigger, your tool is probably reintroducing precision or structure — check the settings before trusting the result. The right measure is not the smallest possible file, but the smallest file that still renders correctly on every target you care about.</p>

schema.headline: The Complete SVG Optimization Guide
schema.description: How to reduce SVG file size through precision, metadata stripping, flattening, and path cleanup.

title: Vectorization Tips: Getting Clean Vectors from Raster Images
seoTitle: Vectorization Tips — How to Trace Raster Images into Clean Vectors
seoDescription: Best practices for raster-to-vector conversion: preparing the source, choosing the right trace mode, tuning parameters, and cleaning up the result.
content:
Raster-to-vector conversion — vectorization, or tracing — turns a grid of pixels into paths. The output can be sharper at any size, editable as individual shapes, and usable for cutting, engraving, and print at large formats. But tracing is not a magic filter: it is a reconstruction problem, and the quality of the result depends mostly on the source image and how the tracing parameters are set. These are the practices that make the difference between a usable vector and a mess of jagged noise.

Start with a source that is worth tracing

The single largest factor in trace quality is input quality. A clean, high-contrast image with a plain background traces well. A small, blurry JPEG with compression artifacts does not — no tracing setting can recover detail that was never there.

  • Resolution — aim for at least 1000 pixels on the long edge, and more for fine detail. Tiny images produce chunky, inaccurate paths.
  • Contrast — silhouettes and flat-color logos trace cleanly; soft gradients and photographs do not.
  • Compression artifacts — JPEG blocks and ringing around edges become spurious paths. Convert to PNG before tracing if possible.
  • Background — remove or flatten the background first. A busy backdrop becomes dozens of shapes nobody wants.

Decide what kind of trace you need

There are three broad modes, and choosing the wrong one wastes more time than any parameter tweak. A silhouette trace produces one outline of a solid shape, which is ideal for logos, icons, and cut files. A color trace produces one path per distinct color region, which suits flat illustrations and screen-print separations. A centerline trace follows the stroke of line art rather than its boundary, which is correct for signatures, technical drawings, and single-line engraving.

Most people who are disappointed with a trace used a color trace when they wanted a silhouette, or a silhouette when the source was line art. Look at the image and ask what the marks are: filled areas should be traced as regions, strokes should be traced as centerlines.

Clean the image before tracing

Spend a minute on preprocessing. Threshold or posterize the image so color boundaries become crisp. Despeckle to remove isolated pixels that would become tiny stray paths. Smooth edges slightly — a half-pixel blur before thresholding often produces cleaner contours than a hard cut. If the image has anti-aliased edges, thresholding at the midpoint keeps the shape truest.

For logos that were scanned from print, straighten the scan and fix perspective first. A 1% rotation becomes a lattice of skewed paths that is difficult to correct later. For photos you intend to keep photographic, accept that a trace will produce an illustrative, posterized version, not a photographic vector.

Tune the tracing parameters deliberately

Every tracer exposes roughly the same controls under different names: a threshold or color count, a noise or speckle filter, a corner versus smooth preference, and a minimum path size. Change one at a time and compare at 100% and 400%.

  • Threshold — the luminance cut between foreground and background. Move it until the silhouette matches the visual edge, not until the histogram looks nice.
  • Colors — fewer colors mean fewer paths and cleaner overlaps. Most logos need two to five.
  • Speckle / noise — raise it until isolated single-pixel islands disappear, but not so far that fine details go with them.
  • Corner threshold — lower values keep sharp corners; higher values round them. Text and technical shapes need sharp corners preserved.
  • Minimum area — discards tiny regions that would otherwise become unprintable slivers.

Fix the result rather than re-traced

Even a good trace produces more nodes than a hand-drawn logo. Resist re-tracing with different settings in hope of a cleaner result; instead edit the output. Delete stray islands, merge overlapping shapes, close gaps, and simplify paths. A smaller node count does more for file size and cutting reliability than any single export option.

If the trace includes a background rectangle, delete it. If shapes overlap when they should meet edge-to-edge, decide whether you need a union or a minus-front operation, and apply it once. For cut files, ensure each shape you intend to cut is a closed path with no self-intersections.

Know what tracing cannot do

Tracing is not a route to perfect geometry. It reconstructs contours, not intent. It cannot know that a slightly wobbly circle was meant to be a perfect circle, that a hand-lettered word should use a specific typeface, or that a texture was a printing artifact. Where those intentions matter, rebuild the shape by hand with proper primitives or replace text with real type.

Likewise, tracing a photograph produces a stylised illustration, not a lens-sharp vector portrait. If someone asks for "the photo as an SVG," clarify whether they want a posterized graphic, a single-color silhouette for engraving, or an embedded raster inside an SVG. Each is a different job with a different result.

A checklist before you accept the trace

  1. View at 100% for overall likeness and at 400% for curve quality.
  2. Confirm there are no stray islands, holes, or hairline slivers.
  3. Check that all text is either live type or cleanly outlined.
  4. Verify the node count is proportionate to the detail.
  5. For cutting, confirm closed paths, no overlaps, and consistent units.
  6. For print, check that colors are flat and there is no unintended transparency.

Tracing rewards patience at the input stage more than cleverness at the output stage. Clean the source, pick the right trace mode, change one parameter at a time, and finish with a short cleanup pass. That sequence consistently produces vectors that are smaller, easier to edit, and more reliable to manufacture.

schema.headline: Vectorization Tips: Getting Clean Vectors from Raster Images
schema.description: Best practices for preparing, tracing, tuning, and cleaning up raster-to-vector conversions.

title: Preparing SVG Files for Cricut
seoTitle: Cricut Design Guide — How to Prepare SVG Files for Cricut
seoDescription: Learn how Cricut Design Space reads SVG geometry and how to prepare closed paths, outlined text, correct sizes, and separate layers for reliable cuts.
content:
Cricut Design Space is forgiving about many things and strict about a few. Uploaded artwork is treated as a cut path, which means the software cares about closed shapes, clean edges, and a sensible physical size far more than it cares about artistic nuance. Most Cricut problems — missing parts of a design, double-cut lines, scores that behave like cuts — trace back to how the SVG was prepared. This guide covers the preparation that prevents them.

What Cricut actually sees in your file

Design Space converts everything you upload into layers of shapes. Closed paths become cuttable areas; open paths may be ignored or, depending on the software version, treated unpredictably. Fills are visual only: a shape filled with color still cuts along its outline, while a shape with no area at all cuts nothing. Strokes are not cut as centre lines the way you might expect — the blade follows the path geometry, so a stroke centred on a path still leaves two passes if the path is an open rectangle rather than a line.

This is why an SVG that renders beautifully in a browser can fail in Design Space. The browser draws strokes; the cutter needs closed regions. Before upload, think in terms of regions and boundaries, not brushes and styles.

Prepare the SVG for cutting

  • Close every path you want cut. Use your editor's close-path command, then verify there are no stray endpoints.
  • Convert strokes to outlines. If a design uses a thick stroked line, expand it into a filled shape so the blade can follow its two edges.
  • Remove hidden layers and unused groups. Design Space may still import them and produce invisible cut lines.
  • Outline text. Live text depends on fonts that Design Space may not have; outlined text cannot reflow or disappear.
  • Delete the background rectangle. A full-page white rectangle becomes a full-page cut.
  • Simplify. Very high node counts slow the software and produce rough curves at small sizes.

Size and units

Design Space works in physical units and defaults to inches for many accounts. An SVG with a viewBox but no physical width and height arrives at an unpredictable size. Set explicit width and height in millimetres or inches in the SVG root, then confirm the dimensions in Design Space after upload and scale deliberately if needed.

Design for the material, not just the screen. Vinyl details narrower than about 1 mm are fragile; small text below roughly 6 mm cap height becomes difficult to weed. If the design will be scaled down on the mat, check that at the final size the smallest feature still has enough material to hold together.

One colour per cut layer

Cricut lets you assign each layer a material colour and then cut layers in sequence. Group shapes by the material they will be cut from, and keep those groups as separate, identifiable layers in the SVG rather than a single merged shape. If everything is one flat colour, Design Space still separates disjoint shapes, but deliberate grouping makes it much easier to keep a multi-colour project organised.

For print-then-cut, the artwork is printed first with registration marks and then cut along a boundary. Keep the cut boundary as a separate shape from the printed artwork, with no outline applied, and leave enough margin around the design for the machine to read the marks.

Score, draw, and cut lines

A Cricut project often needs more than cuts: score lines for folds, draw lines for pens, and perforations. Each is a distinct operation assigned to a line in Design Space, so the SVG must carry them as separate objects with names or colours that help you identify them after upload. Use a consistent colour convention — for example one colour for cut, one for score, one for draw — and rename the layers before uploading.

Keep score lines as simple open lines, not thin closed rectangles. A closed rectangle gets cut twice, once along each long edge, which weakens the fold rather than scoring it.

Common upload failures and fixes

SymptomLikely causeFix
Parts of the design missingUnclosed paths or hidden layersClose paths, unhide and flatten layers
Design imports tiny or hugeNo physical size in the SVGSet width and height in mm or inches
Thin outline around everythingStroke left on a filled shapeRemove stroke or expand it to a fill
Double cut linesDuplicated overlapping pathsUnion or delete duplicates
Text changed or vanishedLive text with missing fontOutline the text
Uneven cuts at cornersToo many nodes or jagged traceSimplify and smooth the path

A pre-upload checklist

  1. Open the SVG and confirm every cut shape is a closed path.
  2. Outline all text and convert stroked lines to filled outlines.
  3. Remove the background, hidden layers, and unused defs.
  4. Set the intended physical size in the SVG root.
  5. Name layers by material or operation so they are easy to map.
  6. Upload, check dimensions at 100%, and do a small test cut before production.

Well-prepared SVG files behave predictably on a Cricut: they import at the right size, separate into the expected layers, and cut exactly the boundaries you drew. Most frustration disappears once the file is treated as geometry meant for a blade rather than artwork meant for a screen.

schema.headline: Preparing SVG Files for Cricut
schema.description: How to prepare SVG geometry, text, sizes, and layers for reliable Cricut cuts.

title: Laser Cutting Files: DXF Specifications and Kerf
seoTitle: Laser Cutting Guide — DXF Specs, Units, and Kerf Compensation
seoDescription: A practical laser cutting file guide: DXF units, path topology, kerf measurement and compensation, minimum features, and clean cut/engrave layers.
content:
Laser cutting and engraving are subtractive processes, and they are unforgiving about units, cut width, and path topology. A file that looks correct on screen can still produce parts that do not fit or cuts that wander off the intended line. The issues are not mysterious; they come from a small set of conventions that every well-prepared DXF respects. This guide covers the specifications that matter and the corrections that make parts come out right.

Why DXF is the default for laser work

DXF is a plain-text CAD interchange format. It stores lines, arcs, polylines, splines, and layers, which map almost directly onto what a laser controller needs: move here, cut to there, raise the head. It has no notion of stroke width or fill colour, so there is no ambiguity about what gets cut. Many laser services accept SVG too, but DXF is the more conservative choice when the receiving software is unknown.

Specify units explicitly

The most common DXF failure is a unit mismatch. A DXF file can declare millimetres, centimetres, inches, or nothing at all. If your file is drawn in millimetres and the machine assumes inches, a 100 mm part becomes a 100 inch part — twenty-five times too large. Always export with an explicit unit declaration and confirm with the service or in the controller software. When in doubt, state the units in the filename or job notes as well.

A simple sanity check: include a known reference dimension in the drawing, such as a 10 mm square in a corner or a note with a measured length. If the reference measures correctly after import, the rest of the file probably will too.

Kerf: the gap the laser removes

Every cut removes material. The width of that removed strip is the kerf, typically 0.1 to 0.4 mm depending on the laser, lens, material, and power. This matters whenever two parts must fit together: a tab intended to fit a slot exactly will be too tight, because the slot is narrower by one kerf and the tab is wider by nothing.

Kerf compensation means offsetting the cut path outward or inward by half the kerf so the final part matches the intended dimension. For outside contours you cut slightly outside the line; for holes, slightly inside. Many laser controllers can apply this automatically if you enter the measured kerf; alternatively, compensate in your design software.

Measure the kerf for your material and machine rather than assuming a value. Cut a test square, measure it with callipers, and compare to the file dimension. Run the test again after changing material, power, or focus.

Path topology that the machine can follow

  • Closed contours. Every shape to be cut must be a closed loop. Open paths may be ignored or interpreted as engraving lines.
  • No self-intersections. A path that crosses itself confuses the cut order and can leave uncut slivers.
  • Join coincident nodes. Nearly-touching endpoints create double cuts and fragile webs of material.
  • Separate cut and engrave layers. Put cuts, scores, and raster engraves on distinct layers named clearly so the operator can assign power and speed per layer.
  • Remove duplicate geometry. Overlapping identical paths cause the laser to cut the same line twice, widening the kerf.

Minimum feature size and spacing

A laser cannot cut details smaller than its spot size, and thin material breaks when the remaining web is too narrow. As a rule of thumb, keep details above 0.5 mm for rigid materials and above 1 mm for thin or brittle ones, and keep the spacing between adjacent cuts at least a kerf and a comfortable margin so the material stays strong. Text below about 5 mm height is better engraved than cut.

Avoid designs where two cut lines run parallel closer than the kerf. The material between them vaporises and the part becomes a single slit rather than two edges. If a detail needs to look thin, engrave it instead of cutting it out.

Engraving versus vector cutting

Vector lines cut; raster fills engrave. In most workflows, the distinction is carried by layer type or colour: a black line layer cuts, a filled shape layer engraves. Decide before export which is which, and keep a separate engraving layer for anything that must not go all the way through, such as text on a panel face.

Engraving resolution is a function of the laser's step-over, not the vector node count. Still, keeping the engraving artwork clean matters: gradients cannot be engraved as gradients, and a photo engrave needs a dithered or halftoned raster with deliberate contrast.

SymptomLikely causeFix
Parts fit too tight or too looseKerf not compensatedMeasure kerf, offset contours by half its width
Part comes out the wrong sizeUnit mismatch in the DXFDeclare units and add a reference dimension
Some outlines not cutOpen paths or duplicate geometryClose contours, remove duplicates
Engraving cuts throughEngrave layer assigned as cutSeparate and label cut versus engrave layers
Thin details crumbleFeature smaller than spot or too little webEnlarge detail or engrave instead of cutting

A practical DXF export checklist

  1. Draw at final size in consistent units and set those units in the file.
  2. Close every cut contour and remove self-intersections and duplicate paths.
  3. Put cut, score, and engrave geometry on separate, clearly named layers.
  4. Measure your machine's kerf for the material and compensate if the design needs an exact fit.
  5. Check minimum feature size and spacing against the material.
  6. Include a reference dimension and note the units in the job notes.
  7. Import the file into the controller once and preview before starting the job.

Laser work rewards files that are simple, explicit, and unambiguous. The geometry should be closed, the units should be stated, and the kerf should be measured rather than assumed. Once those are right, the design translates directly into parts that fit.

schema.headline: Laser Cutting Files: DXF Specifications and Kerf
schema.description: DXF units, path topology, kerf compensation, minimum features, and layer preparation for laser cutting.

title: Embroidery File Formats: DST, PES, and JEF Compared
seoTitle: Embroidery File Formats Explained — DST vs PES vs JEF
seoDescription: Compare DST, PES, and JEF embroidery formats, learn what each stores, how they differ from vector graphics, and how artwork becomes a stitch file.
content:
Embroidery files are not vector graphics, though they are frequently confused with them. A vector describes what a shape looks like; an embroidery file describes how a needle moves to produce it. That difference shapes every decision about formats, conversion, and quality. This guide compares the three formats you will meet most often — DST, PES, and JEF — and explains how to move from artwork to a stitch file that a machine can actually run.

What embroidery formats store

Every embroidery format stores a stitch list: a sequence of needle penetrations, with commands to start, stop, change colour, trim the thread, and move without stitching. What varies between formats is how much else they keep. Some retain design-level metadata such as hoop dimensions, colour sequences, and vector objects; others store only the flattened stitch path. When you convert between them, you are often discarding everything above the stitch level.

DST — the universal baseline

DST (Tajima) is the oldest widely used format and the closest thing embroidery has to a lingua franca. It encodes stitches at three units per millimetre for quarter steps and contains only stitch data and colour-change stops; it does not store colour names, hoop size, or object data. Nearly every commercial machine reads DST, which makes it the safe format for sending jobs to a shop or a third party.

The trade-off is editability. Once converted to DST, the design is a stitch list; adjusting density, pull compensation, or fill angle means regenerating it from an intermediate file, not editing the DST. Keep the source object file alongside any DST you produce.

PES — Brother plus object data

PES is Brother's format and is supported by its domestic and many commercial machines, as well as by most digitizing software. It can store stitches plus design objects, thread palettes, and hoop information, which makes it more convenient during production. Beware that PES versions differ: an older machine may not read a newer PES, and a converter may write only the stitch layer even when the source had objects.

PES is a reasonable delivery format when the receiver works on a Brother machine and expects the convenience of stored colours. For archival or cross-machine handoff, keep a DST as well.

JEF — Janome's route

JEF is Janome's format. Like DST it is largely stitch-oriented, with its own header for hoop size and thread count. Janome software reads it natively; other packages import it but may not preserve every attribute. If your production machine is Janome, JEF is the natural target, and the same rule applies: retain the source design for future edits.

A common practical setup keeps three files per design: a DST for universal delivery, the machine-native format (PES or JEF) for in-house production, and the digitizing source for revisions.

Comparing the three formats

FormatOriginStoresBest for
DSTTajimaStitch list, colour stopsUniversal delivery, shops, older machines
PESBrotherStitches + object data, palette, hoopBrother machines, in-house edits
JEFJanomeStitch list, header metadataJanome machines

From artwork to stitch file

Turning a logo into embroidery is a digitizing job, not a format conversion. The process decides stitch types, underlay, density, pull compensation, and the order in which colors sew. A converter can automate part of it, but the output still needs review, because the same vector can sew beautifully or badly depending on how those decisions are made.

  • Simplify the artwork. Very fine detail cannot be sewn; thin lines collapse into the fabric.
  • Choose stitch types. Satin for lettering and borders, fill for solid areas, run stitch for outlines and details.
  • Add underlay. A base layer stabilises the fabric and gives the top stitches something to sit on.
  • Set density and pull compensation. Dense fills pucker; compensation counters the pull that draws stitches tighter than the vector.
  • Respect minimum sizes. Small text needs larger stitches and simpler shapes than print.
  • Sequence colors. Minimise trims and colour changes by grouping the same thread together.

Sizing and scaling

Embroidery designs are digitized for a size range. Scaling a 4-inch design up to 10 inches stretches every stitch and changes the effective density, often causing puckering or gaps. If you need a different size, re-digitize rather than scale, or keep the scaling modest. This is also why the same logo in two sizes may need two stitch files.

Hoop sizes and machine fields vary. Confirm the design fits the intended hoop with a margin for clamping, and check the format against the machine's supported list before sending a job.

A short handoff checklist

  1. Deliver DST for universal compatibility and the native format for the target machine.
  2. Include a colour sequence with thread names or numbers, since DST stores no names.
  3. State the intended final size and hoop.
  4. Keep the digitizing source with the job so revisions are possible.
  5. Sew a test on scrap fabric of the same type before production.

Embroidery formats are machine instructions, and treating them that way resolves most confusion. Pick DST for compatibility, PES or JEF for the machine you own, and always keep the editable source. The quality of the result is determined in digitizing, not in the file extension.

schema.headline: Embroidery File Formats: DST, PES, and JEF Compared
schema.description: A comparison of DST, PES, and JEF formats and how artwork becomes a machine stitch file.

title: Color Separation for Print and Vinyl
seoTitle: Color Separation Guide — Spot Colors, CMYK, and Trapping
seoDescription: Understand spot colors and CMYK, how separations are made, overprint and knockout, trapping, halftones, and how to review a separation before production.
content:
Colour separation is the craft of turning a full-colour design into the set of inks a production process can actually print. Screen printing, offset printing, and vinyl cutting all build colour from a limited number of solids; a design with continuous tone and gradients must be translated into those solids without losing its intent. Spot colours, CMYK, and the traps between them are the vocabulary of that translation.

Spot colours versus process colours

A spot colour is a specific ink, mixed to a recipe and printed from its own plate or screen. A process colour is built from four inks — cyan, magenta, yellow, and black — printed in overlapping halftone dots to simulate a continuous range. Spot colours are vivid, opaque, and consistent; process colours are flexible and can reproduce photographs and gradients.

Designs that use a handful of flat colours are usually cheaper and sharper in spot. Designs with photographic imagery or many blends need process. Many jobs combine the two: process for the image and a spot for a brand colour that must be exact, sometimes with a spot varnish or white.

How separations are made

A separation is one printing plate or screen per ink. In CMYK work, the image is converted to four channels and halftoned at an angle chosen to avoid moiré. In spot work, each colour becomes its own flat plate. The job of the person preparing the file is to make sure each ink is present exactly once, that colours are named consistently, and that overlapping areas are handled deliberately.

  • Name spot colours exactly — a spot called "Brand Red" is not the same as one called "brand red"; the RIP treats them as separate inks.
  • Convert RGB to the target colour space — a vivid RGB blue may be out of gamut in CMYK and print duller.
  • Check total ink coverage — heavy builds of all four inks can exceed what the press or substrate can dry.
  • Keep black text on one plate — small text in four-colour black fringes when plates are slightly misregistered.

Overprint, knockout, and trapping

When one shape sits on top of another, the printer must decide whether the top ink overprints the bottom or knocks it out. Knockout removes the underlying ink so only the top colour prints; overprint leaves both, letting them combine. Knockout gives cleaner colour but risks a thin light halo if registration drifts between plates. Trapping, or spreading and choking, slightly enlarges one shape into the other to hide that gap.

In vector files, these decisions live in object attributes: overprint fill, overprint stroke, and trapping settings. They are easy to set accidentally and hard to see on screen, so inspect separations in a preview mode that shows each plate independently. A thin white line around every object is the classic symptom of an unintended knockout.

Halftones and line screens

Process colour is printed as dots, and the size and angle of those dots determines how the colour reads. A coarse screen is visible but robust; a fine screen holds detail but needs a smoother substrate. For screen printing, the mesh count sets the achievable line screen: a 110 mesh screen cannot hold a 65 lpi halftone. For vinyl and heat transfer, there is no halftone at all — the design must be reduced to solid shapes, which is a different separation problem.

Spot colour separations for cutting and printing

For cut vinyl, each colour is a separate material, and the design must be split into layers that each cut cleanly. For screen printing, each colour is a screen, and the artwork must be prepared as flat, solid regions with registration marks. Both start from the same step: reduce the design to a deliberate palette of solid colours and assign each region to exactly one ink.

  1. Flatten transparency and gradients into the intended solids.
  2. Assign each colour region to a named spot or to a CMYK build, not to an arbitrary RGB value.
  3. Remove unnecessary colours; every extra ink costs a plate or a screen.
  4. Group and label layers by ink so production can assign them quickly.
  5. Add registration marks and keep them on a non-printing layer.

Colour management basics

RGB is device light; CMYK is ink on substrate; Pantone and similar libraries are named ink recipes. Converting between them is not reversible, and the same CMYK values look different on coated and uncoated stock. Work in the destination colour space from the start when you know the process, or use a colour-managed conversion and proof the result.

For brand colours, request the exact ink reference and keep it recorded. A screenshot of a colour is not a specification; a named or numbered ink is. Where a brand colour must match across media, provide both the spot reference and a process fallback.

Reviewing a separation before production

  • Toggle each plate and confirm the content is what you expect.
  • Check that no ink appears unintentionally in the wrong place.
  • Inspect small type for fringing on four-colour black.
  • Verify overprint and knockout behaviour around overlaps.
  • Confirm the total number of inks matches the quote.
  • Proof on the actual substrate when colour accuracy matters.

Colour separation is the point where a design becomes a manufacturing plan. The work is less about prettiness and more about clarity: one region, one ink; one ink, one named plate. Get that right and the print or cut matches the intent; get it wrong and no amount of tweaking on press fully recovers it.

schema.headline: Color Separation for Print and Vinyl
schema.description: Spot versus process color, separation mechanics, trapping, and reviewing plates before production.

title: Batch Conversion Workflows: Automation That Holds Up
seoTitle: Batch Conversion Workflows — Reliable Vector Automation Tips
seoDescription: Design reliable batch vector conversion pipelines: units of work, idempotency, error handling, validation, naming, concurrency, and useful reporting.
content:
Converting or optimizing one file at a time is fine until you have two hundred. At that point, the work shifts from doing the operation to designing a repeatable process that does it consistently, records what happened, and fails safely when a file is malformed. This guide covers the patterns that make batch vector workflows reliable: how to choose the work split, how to name and track results, how to validate, and how to automate the parts that should never need attention.

Start by defining the unit of work

Every batch has a unit — one file, one page, one colour layer — and the unit determines how you detect completion and failure. If your unit is a file, each item succeeds or fails as a whole, which is simple to track. If your unit is a colour layer inside a file, partial success is possible and you need a result object that records what happened rather than a single pass/fail. Choose the unit before writing anything.

For most vector work the file is the right unit. It keeps reporting simple and matches how designers think about deliverables. Split into sub-units only when an operation genuinely needs to succeed per layer, such as separating a multi-colour design into individually cuttable files.

Make the pipeline idempotent

A batch job will be interrupted, rerun, or accidentally duplicated. An idempotent pipeline produces the same result whether an item is processed once or ten times, so a retry is always safe. The usual technique is to make the output a function of the input plus a content hash, then skip items whose output already exists and matches.

  • Never overwrite the only copy of an input. Write outputs to a separate directory with a predictable name.
  • Key outputs by input path and a hash of the file, so an unchanged file reuses its existing result.
  • Write a manifest that records each processed item and its status, so a rerun can resume.
  • Keep original and optimized versions distinct; do not optimize in place.

Fail loudly, continue quietly

In a batch of hundreds, one bad file should not stop the run. Catch per-item failures, record the error message and the input, and continue. At the end, present a summary: counts of succeeded, skipped, and failed, with a list of the failures. Silence about failures is the most common cause of a batch that "completed" but quietly shipped broken assets.

Classify errors so they are actionable. A malformed SVG is a file problem the owner must fix; a timeout is an infrastructure problem a retry may solve; a missing font is a configuration problem. Different classes want different retry policies and different people to notify.

Validate before and after

Validation on the way in prevents wasted work: check extension, magic bytes, and basic parseability before queueing. Validation on the way out prevents broken deliveries: confirm the output exists, is non-trivially sized, parses, and renders. A before/after size comparison is cheap and catches many silent failures — an output that is much larger or much smaller than the input is worth a second look.

Keep a small set of fixture files with known properties as a regression suite. When a tool or parameter changes, run the fixtures and compare the reports. This catches the subtle case where a settings change improves one file type and breaks another.

Name outputs so they sort

Predictable names make results usable without opening each file. A practical convention encodes the source stem, the operation, and a short suffix: "logo-a_optimized.svg", "poster_svg-to-dxf.dxf". If several variants exist, add a parameter token such as "_precision3". Keep the extension accurate and avoid spaces in names that will be consumed by scripts.

If outputs must be grouped, mirror the input directory structure rather than flattening it. A flat folder of three thousand files is harder to inspect than a tree that matches the source, and mirroring makes it obvious which inputs were skipped.

Choose the right concurrency

Parallelism speeds a batch until it meets a bottleneck — CPU, memory, disk, or an external service. Vector conversion and optimization are usually CPU- and memory-bound, so run a modest number of workers and monitor memory. More workers than cores with a heavy optimizer can thrash, producing slower throughput and occasional out-of-memory failures.

Add backpressure so a slow consumer does not allow an unbounded queue to grow. A working queue that reports depth and throughput is more useful than raw speed, because it tells you whether the batch is moving or stuck.

Report outcomes, not just completion

A useful batch report says what changed: total bytes before and after, per-file savings, node count changes, and any warnings. For optimization work, the aggregate saving is the headline; for conversion work, the number of warnings about outlined text or dropped strokes matters more. Link each row to its output so a reviewer can spot-check quickly.

A minimal automation checklist

  1. Define the unit of work and a status model that allows partial success.
  2. Write outputs beside inputs, never over them, with names that sort.
  3. Key by content hash and maintain a manifest so reruns resume safely.
  4. Catch per-item errors, classify them, and continue the run.
  5. Validate inputs and outputs, and keep fixture files for regressions.
  6. Bound concurrency and expose queue depth and throughput.
  7. Produce an aggregate report and a failure list at the end.

Batch conversion is mostly process design. The individual operation is the easy part; the value comes from running it over hundreds of files without duplicates, silent failures, or lost sources. Build the unit of work, make it idempotent, validate at both ends, and report honestly — then the automation earns its keep.

schema.headline: Batch Conversion Workflows: Automation That Holds Up
schema.description: Patterns for reliable batch conversion: idempotency, validation, naming, concurrency, and reporting.
